terms.definition: A gradient noise function invented by Ken Perlin in 1983 that produces smooth, natural-looking randomness, where nearby points have similar values.
Randomness where every value is chosen independently of its neighbors, so it looks like TV static.
Noise made by picking random heights at grid points and smoothly blending between them. Its peaks and valleys tend to sit on the grid.
Noise made by placing random slopes (gradients) at grid points instead of random heights. Perlin noise and simplex noise are both gradient noise.
The direction and steepness of a slope. In Perlin noise, each lattice point gets a random gradient.
An arrow stored at a grid corner in 2D or 3D Perlin noise. It points in the direction the noise rises from that corner.
A regular grid of points, like the whole numbers on a line or the corners of squares on graph paper.
A way to multiply two arrows into one number: positive when they point the same way, zero when at right angles, negative when opposite. For 2D arrows: a.x·b.x + a.y·b.y.
Estimating a value between two known values by blending them. Linear interpolation (lerp) blends as a + (b − a)·t.
An S-shaped easing function that makes the blend between grid points start and end gently. Perlin's improved noise uses 6t⁵ − 15t⁴ + 10t³.
One layer of noise in a stack. Each new octave usually has double the frequency and half the amplitude of the one before.
How close together the bumps in a noise layer are. Higher frequency means more, smaller features across the same space.
How tall the bumps in a noise layer are, meaning how much that layer adds to the final height.
The number each octave's amplitude is multiplied by (often 0.5). Higher persistence keeps fine detail strong, giving rougher results.
The number each octave's frequency is multiplied by (often 2). It sets how much finer each new layer of detail is.
Adding several octaves of noise, each finer and fainter than the last, to create detail at many scales like real terrain.
The starting number for a pseudo-random generator. The same seed always produces the same sequence, and so the same generated world.
Creating content such as maps, textures, or levels with an algorithm instead of making each piece by hand.
Moving each sample point by a noise value before sampling the noise again, as in noise(p + noise(p)), which creates swirling, fluid patterns.
Ken Perlin's 2001 follow-up to Perlin noise. It uses triangles (simplices) instead of squares, so it runs faster in 3D and higher dimensions and has fewer grid-aligned artifacts.
